..
Issued at 300 PM CST Mon Nov 2 2026

Early this morning, dense cloud cover cloaked the region with strong 
southerly surface and low-level flow. While these conditions are not 
necessarily reflections of more recent observations (notably the 
thinning of cloud cover in the southern portions of our forecast 
area), they symbolize the challenges of the short-term forecast 
which has been marked by hindrances and catalysts alike. Water 
vapor imagery around 2 PM shows the base of the mid-level 
shortwave has made it to the Texas/Oklahoma panhandle with a 
surface cold front/dryline sitting just to the east. East of 
this boundary, in what can be considered the warm sector, strong
southerly flow has pushed dewpoints into the low/mid 60s and 
temperatures into the low/mid 70s. Convective initiation has 
begun in western and central Oklahoma. ACARS soundings out of 
KMCI showcase much weaker instability than what has been noted over
Oklahoma. A few showers and storms storms have been able 
develop in the far western portions of our forecast area this 
afternoon by taking advantage of a strong mid-level jet and weak
elevated instability but remain shallow given the poor 
buoyancy. Continued destabilization throughout the afternoon 
could present an isolated severe threat, but the greater severe 
threat is still expected to arrive later in the evening. Close 
monitoring of the environment in the extreme near term (next 1-2
hours or so) will be necessary. 

Late this afternoon and evening, storms are expected to develop 
along the dryline in portions of Texas and Oklahoma before racing 
northeastward with the mid-level jet. Over time, these storms are 
expected to grow upscale into a linear/QLCS mode. With such a 
powerful mid-level jet, storm motions of 50-60 knots are probable, 
enhancing the typical linear storm mode wind threat. MUCAPE is also 
expected to peak around 500-750 J/kg late this evening with CAMs 
suggesting 3CAPE ~50 J/kg. Cyclonically curved hodographs are also 
progged to elongate over the course of the evening with the HREF 
10th percentile 0-1km SRH exceeding 300 m2/s2 (mean 0-1km SRH ~350 
m2/s2). Needless to say, the forecast environment is certainly 
capable of mesovortex generation; as such, there is an elevated 
threat of brief line-embedded tornadoes this evening. Anomalously 
high PWATs around 1.75" could introduce some minor flooding 
concerns. Given the progressive nature of the incoming system, flash 
flooding concerns will likely be highly localized and limited to 
areas that experience especially heavy downpours in a very short 
amount of time...total accumulations by Tuesday evening are expected 
to be between 1.0-1.5" with locally higher amounts possible. 
Generally lesser accumulations are expected in far northwest and 
central Missouri near US-63. 

The line of storms will continue to progress eastward with a 
diminishing severe threat overnight. Early Tuesday morning, a brief 
restrengthening is possible in the eastern portions of the forecast 
area, generally in the vicinity of the US-63 corridor ahead of the 
cold front. Instability during this time looks especially weak, 
however, and with exceptionally strong deep-layer shear (on the 
order of 60-70 kts), it is hard to imagine that many (if any) 
updrafts will survive long enough to become strong or severe before 
being sheared apart. Elsewhere, there may be some lingering 
scattered post-frontal showers/storms throughout the day.

Much cooler, more seasonal temperatures are expected for the latter 
half of the week with daily highs in the upper 50s to lower 60s 
through the weekend. Some guidance suggests potential another system 
to move through Sunday into Monday while others do not, so trends 
will need to be followed over the coming days.
